questions.q: Pema reverses the strip in Activity 7.1 so that pin IV is the pin nearest the candle flame and pin I is the farthest. The pin that falls third is pin ___.
questions.a: II

questions.q: True or False: A long metal strip is heated at its middle, not at an end, and pins stuck with equal wax are placed 4 cm to the left and 4 cm to the right of the heated spot. The two pins fall at nearly the same time. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Heat passes from the hotter part of the strip to the colder parts on both sides. Both pins are the same distance from the heated spot on the same metal, so heat reaches both lumps of wax together.
s: Verdict: True
Reason or correction: heat spreads from the heated spot to colder parts on both sides, equal distances so equal times

questions.q: Two identical ice cubes are put at the same time on two dishes in a room, one a flat steel plate and the other a wooden board of the same size. Both dishes are at room temperature. Which cube melts first, and why?
questions.a: The cube on the steel plate melts first. Steel is a good conductor, so heat flows through it easily from the surroundings to the colder ice; wood is a poor conductor and passes heat slowly.
o: The cube on the steel plate, because steel passes heat from the surroundings to the ice more easily
The cube on the wooden board, because wood feels warmer to the touch and so holds more heat to give
Both cubes melt together, because both dishes are at the same room temperature, whatever they are made of
The cube on the wooden board, because a poor conductor lets heat pass to the ice faster than steel does

questions.q: Pins are fixed at 5 cm, 10 cm and 15 cm on two strips of equal size, one of metal A and one of metal B. With the same flame at one end, the pins fall at these times: metal A, 30 s, 70 s, 120 s; metal B, 55 s, 130 s, 230 s. Which conclusion do the readings support best?
questions.a: Metal A is the better conductor: at 5, 10 and 15 cm the pin falls sooner on A (30, 70, 120 s) than on B (55, 130, 230 s), so heat reaches each spot faster along A. Particles do not travel along the strip in conduction.
o: Metal A is the better conductor, because the pin at each distance falls sooner on A than on B
Metal B is the better conductor, because its pins take longer to fall and so must hold more heat
The two metals conduct equally well, because every pin eventually falls on both strips
Particles of metal A travel faster along the strip than those of B and carry the heat with them

questions.q: Kabir leaves a steel spoon standing in a glass of ice-cold lassi. After a minute the end he holds feels cold. Which statement explains it best?
questions.a: Conduction is the passing of heat from the hotter part to the colder part. Here the hand is warmer than the lassi, so heat leaves the hand through the spoon. What reaches the hand is not a flow of cold.
o: Heat passes from his warmer hand along the spoon towards the colder lassi, so his hand loses heat
Cold passes from the lassi up the steel, particle to particle, until it finally reaches the end he holds
Cold particles of the lassi climb up the spoon and settle at the end of the spoon that he is holding
The steel makes cold of its own and gives that cold to the hand that touches the spoon end

questions.q: Pema cuts a metal strip into two equal pieces and lays them end to end on the stand with a 1 cm gap of air between them. Pin P is on the far end of the second piece. On the unbroken strip, pin P falls in about 2 minutes. She heats the free end of the first piece with the same flame. What will she most likely see?
questions.a: The heat must cross the gap. Air is a poor conductor and the particles of the two pieces are not in contact, so little heat passes across and the pin falls much later (or not at all).
o: Pin P falls much later, because the heat must cross a layer of air, a poor conductor
Pin P falls at about 2 minutes, because the particles of the first piece jump across the gap
Pin P falls sooner than 2 minutes, because the gap keeps the heat from spreading sideways
Pin P falls at about 2 minutes, because metal passes heat through air as easily as through metal

questions.q: One end of a long metal strip is held in a flame. After 2 minutes thermometers touching the strip at 0, 5, 10 and 15 cm from the heated end read 90, 62, 41 and 30 degrees Celsius. The room is at 30 degrees Celsius. What do these readings show?
questions.a: Temperature falls with distance from the heated end (90, 62, 41) and the 15 cm point is still at the room temperature of 30, so the heat has not reached it yet. This is heat passing from the hotter part to the colder part.
o: Heat is flowing from the hot end to the cold end and has not yet reached the 15 cm point
Heat is flowing from the cold end towards the hot end, because the far end is at room temperature
Particles of the strip have travelled 10 cm from the hot end, which is why that point is above 30 degrees
The strip is carrying the same amount of heat to all four points, because all were read at the same moment

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A strip of wood in Activity 7.1 would let the pins fall one after another, only more slowly than a metal strip does.
Statement 2: If the metal strip is made twice as long, the pin at its far end falls later, because the heat has to be passed on through more of the strip.
Statement 3: When the handle of a spoon in hot tea warms up, no particle of the spoon travels from the tea to the handle.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false: with a wood strip the pins will not fall, since wood is a poor conductor. Statement 2 follows from heat being passed from particle to particle, and Statement 3 is the book's point that particles stay in their positions.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When two metal rods of the same material and thickness, one 10 cm long and one 20 cm long, are held in the same flame, their far ends become hot at the same time.
Reason (R): In conduction a heated particle passes the heat on to its neighbour, so heat needs time to travel farther along the rod.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The Assertion is false: the far end of the longer rod is reached later because the heat has to be passed on through more particles. The Reason is true and in fact contradicts the Assertion.
o: Assertion is false, but Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.

questions.q: Rohan says: 'The handle of an iron tongs left in a coal fire gets hot because the iron carries the heat to the handle the way a bucket carries water.' (a) State what the particles of the tongs actually do. (b) Explain why the handle still becomes too hot to hold.
questions.a: (a) The heated particle passes the heat on to its neighbour, and so on, but the particles themselves stay in their positions; nothing is carried like a bucket. (b) Iron is a good conductor, so heat passes from particle to particle all along the tongs from the fire end to the handle end.
s: Part (a): particles pass heat to neighbours but do not move from their positions
Part (b): iron is a good conductor, so heat passes along to the handle end

questions.q: A rod is made by joining a 10 cm piece of iron end to end with a 10 cm piece of dry wood of the same thickness. A wax dot is placed at the joint and another at the free end of the wood. The free end of the iron is held in a flame. (a) Which dot melts first? (b) Why may the dot on the wood never melt?
questions.a: (a) The dot at the joint. (b) Iron is a good conductor, so heat reaches the joint easily; wood is a poor conductor and does not let heat pass through it easily, so little heat reaches the free end of the wood.
s: Part (a): the dot at the joint melts first
Part (b): wood is a poor conductor, so heat is held back before the far dot

questions.q: After 3 minutes in the same flame, four rods of equal size show these results. Rod A: wax dots at 5 cm, 10 cm and 15 cm all melted. Rod B: dots at 5 cm and 10 cm melted. Rod C: only the dot at 5 cm melted. Rod D: no dot melted. (a) Arrange the rods from the best to the poorest conductor. (b) A cook needs a pan with a handle: which rod should she use for the base and which for the handle? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) A, B, C, D. (b) Base: rod A, a good conductor that passes the flame's heat to the food; handle: rod D, the poorest conductor, which lets almost no heat reach the hand.
s: Part (a): A, B, C, D
Part (b): A for the base, D for the handle, with the conductor reason

questions.q: In a 12 cm metal strip, pins at 3, 6, 9 and 12 cm from the flame fall at 40 s, 100 s, 180 s and 280 s. (a) Find the time gaps between successive pins. (b) If the gaps keep growing by the same amount each time, when would a pin at 15 cm fall?
questions.a: (a) 100 - 40 = 60 s; 180 - 100 = 80 s; 280 - 180 = 100 s. (b) The gaps grow by 20 s each time, so the next gap is 120 s and the pin at 15 cm falls at 280 + 120 = 400 s.
s: Part (a): 60 s, 80 s and 100 s
Part (b): next gap 120 s, so 400 s

questions.q: Ishaan says: 'When one end of a metal rod is heated, heat travels along the rod to the far end by conduction. This happens because the hot particles move along the rod to the cold end.' Is Ishaan right? Say whether he is right, partly right or wrong, and explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Heat does travel along the rod to the far end by conduction, but the reason given is wrong: in conduction the particles do not move from their positions. The heated particle passes heat to its neighbour, and so on, so the heat travels though the particles stay put.
s: Verdict: partly right (heat does travel by conduction, but the reason is wrong)
Particles stay in their positions during conduction
Far end warms because heat is passed neighbour to neighbour

questions.q: Describe one everyday situation, not given in the chapter, in which heat travels by conduction. Say which part is hotter, which part gains heat, and what the particles do.
questions.a: Example: a steel tumbler of hot tea warms the hand held round it. The tea and tumbler wall are hotter, the hand gains heat, and the particles of the steel pass heat to neighbours without leaving their positions. Any valid example with the three points earns full marks.
s: A valid everyday situation of conduction
Hotter part and the part gaining heat identified
Particles pass heat on without moving from their positions

questions.q: Dhruv says that in Activity 7.1 the pins fall because hot air rising from the flame melts the wax, and not because heat travels along the strip. Show that this cannot be the main reason, using what happens when a wooden strip replaces the metal strip.
questions.a: With a wooden strip the flame and the hot air are exactly the same, yet the book says the pins will not fall. So hot air is not what melts the wax. The pins fall on a metal strip because the metal, a good conductor, carries heat along the strip from the heated end, particle to particle, to the wax; wood is a poor conductor and does not.
s: Same flame and hot air with a wooden strip, but the pins do not fall
So the melting is not caused by the hot air
Metal is a good conductor that carries the heat along to the wax; wood is a poor conductor

questions.q: A cook uses iron tongs 30 cm long in a coal fire; after 3 minutes the handle end reads 58 degrees Celsius. Iron tongs of the same thickness but 50 cm long read 41 degrees at the handle end in the same time. The 30 cm tongs with a wooden grip fitted read 33. The room is at 28 degrees. (i) Find how many degrees above the room each handle end is. (ii) Use Activity 7.1 to explain why the longer tongs are cooler at the handle. (iii) Explain the effect of the wooden grip. (iv) The cook must reach 40 cm into the fire. Which tongs should she choose, and why?
questions.a: (i) 58 - 28 = 30, 41 - 28 = 13 and 33 - 28 = 5 degrees. (ii) In Activity 7.1 the pins farther from the flame fall later: heat has to be passed from particle to particle through more of the metal, so less reaches the handle in the same time. (iii) Wood is a poor conductor, so the grip lets very little heat reach the hand. (iv) The 30 cm tongs cannot reach 40 cm, so she should choose the 50 cm tongs, whose handle is 17 degrees cooler than the 30 cm iron tongs.
s: Part (i): 30, 13 and 5 degrees above the room
Part (ii): farther along the metal, heat reaches later and less, as pins farther from the flame fall later
Part (iii): wood is a poor conductor so little heat reaches the hand
Part (iv): 50 cm tongs because 30 cm cannot reach 40 cm
Part (iv): handle is 17 degrees cooler (58 - 41) than the shorter iron tongs

questions.q: Design a fair test to find out which of two metals, X or Y, is the better conductor of heat, using strips, wax and pins as in Activity 7.1. Say what you will keep the same, what you will change, what you will observe, how you will decide, and one safety precaution.
questions.a: Keep the same: strip length and thickness, the number and spacing of the pins, the wax, and the flame (and how far its end is held in it). Change only the metal: one strip of X and one of Y. Observe the time at which each pin falls on each strip. Decide: the metal whose pins fall sooner at the same distances is the better conductor. Precaution: perform the activity under the supervision of a teacher or an adult, as the book cautions.
s: Controlled: same size, pin spacing, wax and flame
Only the metal is changed
Observation: the times at which the pins fall
Decision rule: pins falling sooner means the better conductor
Safety: carry out under supervision of a teacher or adult

questions.q:
A cookware maker in Ludhiana tests two metal sheets for pan bases. Equal strips are heated at one end with wax dots at 5, 10 and 15 cm. Sheet M1 (Rs 260 per pan): dots melt at 40 s, 90 s and 160 s. Sheet M2 (Rs 200 per pan): dots melt at 70 s, 150 s and 270 s. The maker's rule: the 15 cm dot must melt within 4 minutes, or the pan cooks too slowly. An order is for 50 pans.
(a) How much longer than the 5 cm dot does the 15 cm dot take on each sheet?
(b) Which sheet is the better conductor, and how do the times show it?
(c) Explain, in terms of particles, how heat reached the 15 cm dot.
(d) Which sheet should the maker use? Work out the difference in cost for 50 pans and weigh it against the rule.
questions.a: (a) M1: 160 - 40 = 120 s; M2: 270 - 70 = 200 s. (b) M1; the dot at every distance melts sooner on M1. (c) Each heated particle passed the heat to its neighbour, and so on along the sheet, while the particles stayed in their positions. (d) M1: 60 x 50 = Rs 3,000 more for the order, but M2's 15 cm dot takes 270 s, more than 4 minutes (240 s), so M2 breaks the rule and the saving is not acceptable.
s: Part (a): 120 s and 200 s
Part (b): M1, as its dots melt sooner at every distance
Part (c): heat handed from particle to neighbour with particles staying in position
Part (d): Rs 3,000 more for M1, and M2 fails the 4-minute rule so M1 is chosen

questions.q:
The canteen of a school in Nagpur tests three spoons of equal length for stirring boiling sambar. After two minutes in the pot the handle end of each is measured. Spoon P (all steel, Rs 40 each): 61 degrees Celsius. Spoon Q (steel with a wooden handle, Rs 65 each): 34. Spoon R (all wood, Rs 90 each): 33. The room is at 30 degrees. The canteen needs 12 spoons, has Rs 1,200, and will accept only spoons whose handle end stays within 8 degrees of the room temperature.
(a) How many degrees above the room temperature is the handle end of each spoon?
(b) Explain the reading of spoon P, naming the process.
(c) Spoon Q is dipped in the same pot, yet its handle stays at 34. Explain why.
(d) Find the cost of 12 of each type and decide which spoon the canteen should buy, using the rule and the budget.
questions.a: (a) P 31, Q 4, R 3 degrees. (b) Conduction: steel is a good conductor, so heat is passed from particle to particle up to the handle. (c) The steel part conducts heat up to the joint, but the wooden handle is a poor conductor and lets little heat pass on to the end that is held. (d) 12 of P cost Rs 480, Q Rs 780, R Rs 1,080. P breaks the rule (31 is more than 8). Q and R both pass the rule and both fit Rs 1,200, but R costs Rs 300 more for a handle only 1 degree cooler. Buy Q.
s: Part (a): 31, 4 and 3 degrees above the room
Part (b): conduction along a good conductor
Part (c): wooden handle is a poor conductor so little heat passes on
Part (d): Rs 480, 780 and 1,080; P fails the rule; Q chosen over R for Rs 300 less with a similar handle

questions.q: True or False: A thick woollen blanket that has been pressed completely flat, squeezing out the air held in its fabric, keeps us just as warm as when it is fluffy. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Wool keeps us warm because its fabric traps air, and air is a poor conductor that reduces heat flow from the body. With the air squeezed out, less poor-conducting air is held, so more heat flows away from the body.
s: Verdict: False
Reason or correction: Wool keeps us warm because its fabric traps air, and air is a poor conductor that reduces

questions.q: Sunita covers a steel tumbler of hot tea with a flat steel plate. Her brother says a wooden board would be a better cover for keeping heat in. (a) Which of the two materials lets heat pass out through the cover more easily? (b) Whose suggestion is better as far as conduction goes? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The steel plate. (b) The brother's: wood is a poor conductor, so less of the tea's heat passes out through a wooden cover, whereas steel, a good conductor, lets it pass easily.
s: Part (a): steel plate lets heat pass more easily
Part (b): wooden board, a poor conductor, is better for keeping the tea hot

questions.q: Rohan's tea is too hot to drink before school. He pours 85 degrees Celsius tea into a steel tumbler and an identical amount into a clay cup. After 5 minutes the steel tumbler's tea reads 61 and the clay cup's tea reads 74. (a) Find the fall in temperature in each. (b) Which one should he use to cool his tea quickly, and why?
questions.a: (a) Steel 85 - 61 = 24 degrees; clay 85 - 74 = 11 degrees. (b) The steel tumbler: steel is a good conductor and lets the heat out faster, while clay is a poor conductor and keeps the tea hot longer.
s: Part (a): 24 and 11 degrees
Part (b): steel, a good conductor, lets heat out faster

questions.q: A vendor wraps a big slab of ice in a thick woollen blanket on a hot day. (a) Will the wrapped slab melt more slowly than a bare one? (b) Use the book's reason for why wool keeps us warm to explain your answer.
questions.a: (a) Yes, it melts more slowly. (b) Woollen fabric traps air in its pores and air is a poor conductor of heat. Just as it reduces heat flow from our body to the surroundings, it reduces heat flow from the hot surroundings into the ice.
s: Part (a): the wrapped slab melts more slowly
Part (b): trapped air is a poor conductor, so less heat flows in

questions.q: On a night when it is 3 degrees Celsius outside, a hill family's room with walls of wooden layers filled with mud is at 16 degrees. After the walls are replaced by thin iron sheets, the same room on a similar night is at 6 degrees. (a) By how many degrees did the amount by which the room is warmer than outside change? (b) Give the reason for the change.
questions.a: (a) Before: 16 - 3 = 13 degrees above outside; after: 6 - 3 = 3 degrees; the difference fell by 10 degrees. (b) Iron is a good conductor, so heat escapes through the iron sheets quickly, while wood and mud are poor conductors that prevent heat loss.
s: Part (a): 13 and 3 degrees above outside, a fall of 10
Part (b): iron is a good conductor; wood and mud are poor conductors

questions.q: Hot milk at 85 degrees Celsius is kept in three ways for 15 minutes. A single steel tumbler cools to 49. The same tumbler placed inside a second steel tumbler, with a thin layer of air between them, cools to 61. Which conclusion is best supported by these readings?
questions.a: The fall is 85 - 49 = 36 degrees for one tumbler and 85 - 61 = 24 for the pair. The only change is the layer of air between the tumblers, a poor conductor, which slows the loss of heat. Steel is the same good conductor in both.
o: The air layer cut the fall from 36 to 24 degrees, which fits air being a poor conductor
Two steel tumblers lose heat faster than one, because two good conductors pass heat twice as fast
The second tumbler is a poor conductor, which is why the milk in the pair lost less heat
The milk in the pair lost no heat, because the air between the tumblers is a good conductor

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Metal utensils are chosen for cooking, yet tea is often served in clay cups.
Reason (R): In cooking, heat must pass quickly from the flame to the food, whereas a drink in a cup should lose its heat slowly.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: good conductors (metals) pass the flame's heat to the food quickly, while clay is a poor conductor and lets the heat of the tea leave only slowly.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

questions.q: On a hot afternoon a fruit seller in Nagpur wraps his bottles of cold water in a woollen cloth. A customer says wool is meant only for winter. Which reply is correct?
questions.a: The same trapped air that reduces heat flow from our body in winter also reduces heat flow into the bottle in summer. The poor conductor slows the heat in either direction.
o: Wool traps air, a poor conductor, which slows the heat flowing in, so the water stays cold longer
Wool is a good conductor, so it spreads the cold of the water evenly through the whole bottle and cloth
Wool reflects most of the heat falling on it, so almost no sunlight ever reaches the bottle
Wool gives out cold of its own, and this cold is added to the water in the bottle

questions.q: A mason in a hill town fills the holes of the hollow bricks of a school wall with iron pieces to make the wall stronger. How will the room in winter compare with a room built of unfilled hollow bricks?
questions.a: The room will be colder. The hollow bricks keep a house warm because of the air trapped in them, a poor conductor. Replacing it with iron, a good conductor, lets heat pass through the wall more easily.
o: Colder, because trapped air, a poor conductor, is replaced by iron, a good conductor
Warmer, because iron is heavy and so holds more of the room's heat inside the wall
The same, because the bricks around the holes are unchanged and still make up the wall
Colder, because iron produces cold of its own and passes that cold into the room

questions.q: In which of these is the poor conduction of air trapped in a material NOT the main reason why heat is held back?
questions.a: In the clay cup the clay itself is the poor conductor and it is a solid material. In the other three, air trapped in wool, between blankets or in the holes of the bricks is what slows the heat.
o: Tea stays hot longer in a clay cup than in a steel tumbler
A woollen jersey keeps a child warm on a cold morning
Two thin blankets keep a sleeper warmer than one thick blanket
Hollow bricks help keep a classroom cool in summer

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Tea poured into a steel tumbler loses heat faster than the same tea in a clay cup of the same size, because steel lets heat pass out more easily.
Statement 2: A Himalayan wall of two wooden layers filled with cow dung and mud helps to keep a house warm because wood and mud do not let heat escape easily.
Statement 3: Air trapped in hollow bricks keeps a house warm in winter, but makes no difference to how hot it gets in summer.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: the trapped air, a poor conductor, slows heat flow in both directions, so hollow bricks keep houses warm in winter and cool in summer.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Hot tea at 90 degrees Celsius is poured into a steel tumbler and into a clay kulhad of the same size. After 10 minutes the steel tumbler reads 54 and the kulhad reads 72. The tea in the steel tumbler has lost ___ times as many degrees as the tea in the kulhad.

Match the situation in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. A bottle of cold water wrapped in woollen cloth on a hot day; 2. A wooden handle on a steel pan; 3. Tea in a clay kulhad; 4. A thin iron sheet used as the wall of a hill house.
Column II: a. Heat from the pan is held back from the hand; b. Heat leaves the drink only slowly through the material; c. Trapped air slows the heat coming in from the surroundings; d. The material lets the heat of the room escape easily.
questions.a: 1 wrapped bottle - c (trapped air in wool slows the heat coming in); 2 wooden handle - a; 3 clay kulhad - b; 4 iron sheet wall - d (a good conductor). The other pairings swap the directions of heat flow.

questions.q: Imran says: 'A wall built of two layers of brick with a sealed gap of still air between them should keep a room warmer than a single solid layer of the same bricks, because air is a poor conductor.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. Air is a poor conductor of heat, so the sealed layer of still air slows the flow of heat through the wall, as the air trapped in hollow bricks and between two thin blankets does. The wall with the gap therefore loses less heat in winter.
s: Verdict: agrees
Air is a poor conductor of heat
The trapped layer of air slows heat flow, like hollow bricks and the air between two blankets

questions.q: Describe one situation, not given in the chapter, in which a poor conductor is used to keep heat out of something. Name the poor conductor, say what heat flow it slows down and give the reason it works.
questions.a: Example: a vendor keeps ice-cream or cold drinks in a box lined with woollen cloth. The wool, with air trapped in its pores, is a poor conductor; it slows the flow of heat from the hot surroundings into the box, so the contents stay cold longer. Any valid situation with these three points earns full marks.
s: A valid situation using a poor conductor to keep heat out
Poor conductor named and the heat flow it slows stated
Reason: a poor conductor lets heat pass only with difficulty

questions.q: A shopkeeper says: 'A steel tumbler is the best way to keep tea hot for a long time, because metals are good conductors.' Show that this reasoning cannot work.
questions.a: A good conductor lets heat pass out of the tea easily, so the tea would lose heat quickly. The book says tea in clay or porcelain cups stays hot longer because they are poor conductors. So being a good conductor does not help to keep tea hot.
s: Good conductors let heat pass easily, so heat leaves the tea
Clay or porcelain (poor conductors) keep tea hot longer
Concludes that the shopkeeper's reasoning is wrong

questions.q:
At a 12-day winter fair in Mussoorie, Meena serves 200 cups of tea a day at 80 degrees Celsius. She can use steel tumblers (Rs 22 each, reused for all 12 days), clay kulhads (Rs 3 each, thrown away after one use), or a steel tumbler placed inside a second steel tumbler (Rs 22 and Rs 10, reused). Ten minutes after pouring, the tea reads 52 degrees in a steel tumbler, 66 in a kulhad and 63 in the pair of tumblers. Meena's rule: the tea must still be above 60 degrees after 10 minutes, and she wants the cheapest choice that meets this.
(a) By how many degrees did the tea cool in each container?
(b) Why did the tea cool less in the kulhad than in the steel tumbler?
(c) Why did the pair of tumblers keep the tea hotter than one tumbler?
(d) Work out the cost of each choice for 200 cups and the 12 days, and decide which she should use.
questions.a: (a) 28, 14 and 17 degrees. (b) Clay is a poor conductor, so it lets heat pass out only slowly, while steel is a good conductor. (c) The layer of air trapped between the two tumblers is a poor conductor and slows the loss of heat. (d) Steel tumblers 200 x 22 = Rs 4,400 but 52 is not above 60, so they fail. Kulhads 200 x 3 x 12 = Rs 7,200. The pair of tumblers 200 x (22 + 10) = Rs 6,400. Both kulhads and the pair meet the rule; the pair is Rs 800 cheaper, so she should use the pair of tumblers.
s: Part (a): 28, 14 and 17 degrees
Part (b): clay is a poor conductor, steel a good conductor
Part (c): trapped air between the tumblers is a poor conductor
Part (d): Rs 4,400 (fails), Rs 7,200 and Rs 6,400; the pair of tumblers is the cheapest that meets the rule

questions.q:
A Himalayan village school is choosing between two buildings. House X, with walls of two wooden layers filled with cow dung and mud, cost Rs 2,40,000; on a night when it is 2 degrees Celsius outside its room is at 14 degrees. House Y, built of hollow bricks, cost Rs 1,90,000 and its room is at 13 degrees. The school has Rs 2,50,000 and is used in all seasons, including hot summers.
(a) By how many degrees is the room in each house warmer than the outside?
(b) Explain why the room in House X stayed warm.
(c) Explain why hollow bricks can help the school in summer as well as in winter.
(d) Which house should the school choose? Weigh the temperatures, the cost and the use in all seasons.
questions.a: (a) X: 14 - 2 = 12 degrees; Y: 13 - 2 = 11 degrees. (b) Wood and mud are poor conductors, so they prevent heat loss. (c) The air trapped in the holes is a poor conductor, so it slows heat flowing out in winter and flowing in during summer. (d) House Y: both houses are within Rs 2,50,000, but Y costs Rs 50,000 less (2,40,000 - 1,90,000), is only 1 degree cooler in winter, and also keeps the rooms cool in summer. The wall of X is described for staying warm in winter only.
s: Part (a): 12 and 11 degrees
Part (b): wood and mud are poor conductors that prevent heat loss
Part (c): trapped air slows heat flow in both directions
Part (d): House Y, weighing Rs 50,000 and 1 degree against use in all seasons

questions.q: A hill school plans a new classroom with 60 square metres of outer wall. Design A: two wooden layers filled with cow dung and mud, Rs 1,100 per square metre; on a night with 2 degrees Celsius outside, such a room reaches 12 degrees. Design B: hollow bricks, Rs 1,400 per square metre; reaches 13 degrees. Design C: thin iron sheets, Rs 600 per square metre; reaches 5 degrees. The school wants the cheapest design that keeps the room at 12 degrees or more on such a night. Evaluate the three designs and recommend one.
questions.a: Costs: A 60 x 1,100 = Rs 66,000; B 60 x 1,400 = Rs 84,000; C 60 x 600 = Rs 36,000. C is cheapest but reaches only 5 degrees: iron is a good conductor and lets heat escape, so it fails the rule. A is warm because wood and mud are poor conductors; B because air trapped in the hollow bricks is a poor conductor. Both A and B meet 12 degrees, and B costs Rs 18,000 more for 1 degree extra. Recommend A, the cheapest design that meets the rule.
s: Costs worked out: Rs 66,000, 84,000 and 36,000
C fails the rule (5 degrees) because iron is a good conductor
A and B keep heat in because wood and mud, and trapped air, are poor conductors
B costs Rs 18,000 more for only 1 degree extra
Recommends A as the cheapest design meeting 12 degrees

questions.q: A student answers a question on hollow bricks: 'Hollow bricks are used in hot regions because the holes make the bricks lighter, so they cannot soak up the heat of the Sun. They keep houses cool in summer. In winter such a house will be cold because the holes let the cold in.' Evaluate this answer: say which part is correct, which parts are wrong, and give a corrected explanation.
questions.a: Correct: hollow bricks help keep a house cool in summer. Wrong: the holes are not important because they make the bricks lighter. The air trapped in the holes is a poor conductor of heat, which slows heat flowing into the house. Also wrong: the house is not cold in winter, since the same trapped air slows the heat flowing out, so hollow bricks keep houses warm in winter and cool in summer. The cold does not enter; heat leaves, and the poor conductor slows it.
s: Identifies the correct part: cooler in summer
Rejects the lighter-bricks reason and gives trapped air, a poor conductor
Rejects the claim that the house is cold in winter: it is kept warm
Explains that the poor conductor slows heat flow in either direction
Gives a clear corrected explanation

questions.q: In Activity 7.3 Divya places the candle just below the left edge of the beaker's base instead of the centre, with the grain of potassium permanganate still at the centre of the base. Which description of the movement of the water is best?
questions.a: Water rises where it is heated, here at the left edge, becoming lighter as it expands. Cooler, heavier water comes down elsewhere to replace it, so the circulation is centred on the heated side.
o: Water rises on the left where it is heated, and cooler, heavier water sinks on the right
Water rises at the centre as before, because the grain is at the centre of the base
Water rises on the right, away from the flame, because hot water pushes the cooler water up
Water stays still at the centre, because heat can reach it only by conduction through the glass

questions.q: A thermometer near the top of a tank of water, heated from below, reads 24 degrees Celsius at the start, 26 after 4 minutes and 38 after 10 minutes. In the last 6 minutes the top water warmed ___ times as fast, per minute, as in the first 4 minutes.

Read the statements.
Statement 1: In Activity 7.3 the coloured streak rises near the walls of the beaker and sinks in the middle.
Statement 2: Convection can carry heat along a solid iron rod, because the iron particles move from the hot end to the cold end.
Statement 3: In a beaker heated from below, cooler and heavier water comes down to take the place of the heated water that rises, and the cycle continues until all the water is heated.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only Statement 3 is correct. Statement 1 reverses the streak: it goes up in the middle, above the flame, and comes down at the sides. Statement 2 is false: particles of a solid do not move from their positions, and heat in solids is mainly transferred by conduction.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q: In an Activity 7.2 set-up the stick is horizontal. Isha lights a candle below the left cup and the left cup rises, tilting the stick. She then lights an identical candle below the right cup as well. After both candles have burned together for several minutes, what will she most likely see?
questions.a: Both cups now have warmed air that expands and becomes lighter, so both are lifted by about the same amount and the stick levels out again. Heat is not 'kept' by one cup; both cups are in the same situation.
o: The stick returns close to horizontal, because both cups now hold warmed, lighter air
The right cup rises higher than the left, because it was the cup that was heated second
The stick stays tilted, because the left cup keeps all the heat it received first and stays up
Both cups sink, because two candles together make the air under the cups heavier than before

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A pot of dal gets heated all the way through, although only its base is over the flame.
Reason (R): In liquids, heat is passed from one particle to the next while the particles stay in their positions, as in a metal rod.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The Assertion is true: the dal is heated through by convection, with heated dal rising and cooler dal coming down. The Reason is false: particles staying in their positions describes conduction in solids, whereas in liquids the particles themselves move.
o: Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

questions.q: In which of these is heat NOT carried mainly by the movement of the particles of a liquid or a gas?
questions.a: In the steel ladle the heat is passed from particle to particle of a solid, whose particles stay in place: conduction. The other three involve heated water, air or smoke moving.
o: The handle of a steel ladle left in boiling dal slowly warms up
Water at the top of a beaker warms up when a candle burns below its base
Warm air collects near the ceiling above a burning heater
Smoke from a burning incense stick climbs towards the ceiling

questions.q: Two identical tanks of water at 26 degrees Celsius are heated for 10 minutes, tank A by a heating rod fixed near the bottom and tank B by an identical rod fixed near the top. At the end, tank A reads 48 near the top and 52 near the bottom; tank B reads 52 near the top and 29 near the bottom. Which conclusion do the readings support?
questions.a: In A, water heated at the bottom expands, becomes lighter and rises, while cooler water comes down, so the tank warms evenly (gap 4 degrees). In B the heated water is already at the top, so nothing carries the heat down (gap 23 degrees).
o: In A the heated water rose and spread the heat; in B it stayed at the top, so the bottom barely warmed
Heat travels downwards through water faster than it travels upwards, so tank B should have warmed more evenly
The rod in tank B gave out more heat than the rod in tank A, which is why its top is hotter
In both tanks the heat reached the far end only by particle-to-particle passing, so the readings differ by chance

questions.q: The freezer compartment of a refrigerator sits at the top, and food on the lower shelves still stays cold. Which statement explains how the cold reaches the lower shelves?
questions.a: Cooler air is heavier and sinks, as cooler water comes down in the beaker, while the warmer air rises. This movement of air currents carries the cooling through the compartment.
o: Air cooled by the freezer becomes heavier and sinks, while warmer air from below rises
Cold air is lighter than warm air, so it rises from the freezer and settles on the lower shelves
Heat passes up through the shelves by conduction until the whole refrigerator is equally cold
The cold particles of the freezer air stay in place and pass their cold to the shelf below

questions.q: Arun says: 'In Activity 7.3 the streak of colour rises in the middle because the grain of potassium permanganate is lighter than water.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The grain sits at the base and its colour dissolves in the water. The streak rises because the water at the base is heated by the candle, expands, becomes lighter and rises, carrying the colour with it; cooler, heavier water from the sides comes down. The streak shows the movement of the water.
s: Verdict: disagrees
The heated water at the base expands, becomes lighter and rises, carrying the colour
Cooler, heavier water from the sides comes down: the streak shows water movement, not a light grain

questions.q: Describe a situation at home, not given in the chapter, in which heat is transferred by convection in a liquid or a gas. Explain it by saying what happens to the heated particles.
questions.a: Example: tea boiling in a pan. The tea at the bottom is heated, expands, becomes lighter and rises, and cooler heavier tea from the sides comes down. The heat is carried by the actual movement of the particles. Any valid example with these points earns full marks.
s: A valid situation involving a liquid or gas
Heated particles rise because they expand and become lighter
Cooler particles come down; heat carried by the moving particles

questions.q: Show that convection cannot be the main way in which heat travels along the metal strip in Activity 7.1.
questions.a: Convection is heat transfer by the actual movement of particles of liquids and gases. The particles of a solid strip do not move from their positions, so heat cannot be carried by moving particles. In solids heat is mainly transferred by conduction.
s: Convection needs particles to move from place to place
Particles of a solid strip stay in their positions
So the heat in solids travels mainly by conduction

questions.q: Bhavna lights an incense stick in her room. (a) Give the book's reason for the smoke rising. (b) Explain why the smoke would still rise if the stick were fixed pointing downwards.
questions.a: (a) Smoke is a mixture of hot gases and tiny solid particles, and it is warmer than the surrounding air, so it rises. (b) The direction in which the stick points does not matter: the smoke leaves the burning tip warmer than the air around, so it still moves upwards.
s: Part (a): smoke is warmer than the surrounding air, so it rises
Part (b): it rises even if the stick points down, because of its warmth, not the stick's direction

questions.q: True or False: A room heater fixed close to the ceiling warms the air of the whole room as well as a heater placed near the floor does. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Air heated by the heater expands, becomes lighter and rises. A heater near the floor sets up convection currents that carry the warmth through the room, but air heated near the ceiling stays up there and the air near the floor is left cool.
s: Verdict: False
Reason or correction: Air heated by the heater expands, becomes lighter and rises. A heater near the floor sets

questions.q: The bukhari of a Himalayan home has a long pipe fixed to the top of the stove to vent the smoke. (a) Why does smoke go up the pipe without being pushed? (b) Why would a pipe leading downwards from the bottom of the stove work poorly?
questions.a: (a) Smoke is warmer than the surrounding air, so it rises up the pipe. (b) A downward pipe would ask the warm smoke to move against its tendency to rise, so it would not leave the room well.
s: Part (a): warm smoke rises, so it goes up the pipe
Part (b): downward pipe works against the rising of warm smoke

questions.q: A tank is heated at the bottom. Readings at 2, 8 and 15 minutes: bottom 45, 52 and 55 degrees Celsius; top 26, 48 and 54. (a) Find the difference between bottom and top at each time. (b) What does the shrinking difference show about how the heat reaches the top?
questions.a: (a) 45 - 26 = 19; 52 - 48 = 4; 55 - 54 = 1 degree. (b) Heated water from the bottom rises and carries the heat upward while cooler water comes down, so the top gradually catches up with the bottom.
s: Part (a): 19, 4 and 1 degrees
Part (b): heat is carried upward by moving heated water, so the gap closes

questions.q: Sana leaves a partly inflated balloon in the Sun for an hour, and it has grown larger though no air was added. (a) Explain why it grew. (b) Use your answer to explain why the air around a candle flame rises.
questions.a: (a) The air inside was heated, so it expanded and occupied more space. (b) Air heated by the flame expands in the same way, becomes lighter than the surrounding air and rises.
s: Part (a): heated air expands and occupies more space
Part (b): the air around the flame expands, becomes lighter and rises

questions.q: A beaker of water is heated by a candle under the centre of its base. Readings at 0, 2, 6, 12 and 20 minutes: bottom 26, 45, 50, 52 and 53 degrees Celsius; top 26, 27, 38, 50 and 53. (i) Find the difference between bottom and top at each time. (ii) At what time is the difference the greatest, and why is the top still cool then? (iii) Name the process by which the top gets heated and describe what the water does. (iv) Explain why the water at the sides is part of this process. (v) Explain why the difference becomes zero by 20 minutes.
questions.a: (i) 0, 18, 12, 2 and 0 degrees. (ii) At 2 minutes; the water heated at the base has only just begun to rise, so little heat has reached the top. (iii) Convection: water at the base is heated, expands, becomes lighter and rises, carrying heat upward. (iv) Cooler, heavier water at the sides comes down to take its place and is heated in turn. (v) The cycle continues until the whole volume of water is heated, so the top reaches the bottom's temperature.
s: Part (i): 0, 18, 12, 2 and 0 degrees
Part (ii): greatest at 2 minutes, with the heated water only starting to rise
Part (iii): convection, with heated water expanding and rising
Part (iv): cooler, heavier water from the sides comes down and is heated in turn
Part (v): the cycle continues until the whole water is heated, so both ends are equal

questions.q: A student says: 'A steel spoon kept in a pot of boiling water shows only conduction.' Evaluate this statement using conduction and convection and give your verdict.
questions.a: Heat travels up the steel spoon by conduction, particle to particle, with the particles staying in place. The water in the pot is heated by convection, with hot water rising and cooler water coming down. So the pot shows both processes, and the statement with 'only' is not correct. Both need a medium.
s: Spoon: heat travels by conduction
Particles of the spoon stay in position
Water: heated by convection with moving water
Both processes need a medium
Verdict: the statement is not correct

questions.q:
A student group in Hyderabad heats a beaker of water with a candle below the centre of its base. All the water starts at 28 degrees Celsius. After 4 minutes a thermometer near the base reads 36 and one near the top reads 29. After 10 minutes the base reads 41 and the top reads 38. During the heating, a streak of dye is seen rising in the middle of the beaker and sinking near its walls. Isha says: 'The top water got warm because heat was passed up through the water from particle to particle, with the water staying where it is.'
(a) By how much did the top water warm in the first 4 minutes, and in the next 6 minutes, and how many times faster per minute was the second period?
(b) What does the faster warming of the top show about how the heat was reaching it?
(c) Name the process and explain how the water moves.
(d) Judge Isha's statement using the dye streak and your answers.
questions.a: (a) 29 - 28 = 1 degree in 4 minutes (0.25 per minute); 38 - 29 = 9 degrees in 6 minutes (1.5 per minute): 6 times as fast. (b) Heated water was reaching the top in larger quantity as time passed, carrying the heat with it. (c) Convection: water at the base expands, becomes lighter and rises, while cooler, heavier water from the sides comes down. (d) Isha is wrong: passing heat from particle to particle with the particles staying in place is conduction, but the dye streak shows the water itself moving up and down, so the heat is carried by moving water.
s: Part (a): 1 and 9 degrees, 6 times faster
Part (b): heated water arriving at the top carries the heat
Part (c): convection, rising heated water and sinking cooler water
Part (d): rejects Isha because the dye streak shows the water moving, which conduction does not involve

questions.q:
A school in Pune tests smoke alarm positions in a hall with a 4 m high ceiling. A small incense stick is lit in the middle of the room. A sensor on the ceiling sounds after 14 seconds, one on the wall at 2.5 m after 31 seconds, and one on the wall near the floor after 52 seconds. A sensor costs Rs 1,200. The ceiling can be reached for fitting and monthly testing only with a ladder costing Rs 2,500 (bought once); the 2.5 m position needs no ladder. The school has Rs 4,000 and insists that the alarm must sound within 20 seconds.
(a) By how many seconds did the 2.5 m sensor sound after the ceiling sensor, and the floor sensor after the 2.5 m one?
(b) Explain why the sensors sounded in this order.
(c) Name the process that carries the smoke upward, and say how it differs from heat travelling along a metal rod.
(d) Which position should the school choose? Check each position against the 20-second rule and the budget.
questions.a: (a) 31 - 14 = 17 seconds; 52 - 31 = 21 seconds. (b) Smoke is hot gases and tiny solid particles, warmer than the surrounding air, so it rises and reaches the higher sensors first. (c) Convection: the particles themselves move and carry the heat; in a metal rod (conduction) the particles stay in place and pass the heat on. (d) The ceiling: it is the only position that sounds within 20 seconds (14 s; the 2.5 m position takes 31 s and the floor 52 s), and the cost is 1,200 + 2,500 = Rs 3,700, within Rs 4,000. The cheaper wall position is rejected because it fails the 20-second rule.
s: Part (a): 17 and 21 seconds
Part (b): warm smoke rises, so the higher sensors are reached first
Part (c): convection, with moving particles, unlike conduction
Part (d): ceiling, the only position within 20 s, costing Rs 3,700 within the budget

questions.q: Kavya says: 'On the beach, the wind blows from the sea in the afternoon because the sea is hotter than the land, and the hot sea air pushes in.' Is Kavya right? Say whether she is right, partly right or wrong, and explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The wind does blow from the sea towards the land in the afternoon (a sea breeze), but the reason is wrong. In the daytime the land is warmer than the sea, so the warm air above the land rises and the cooler air from the sea moves in to take its place.
s: Verdict: partly right (direction correct, reason wrong)
The land, not the sea, is warmer in the day, so air above the land rises
Cooler sea air moves towards the land to replace it

questions.q: A student says that in Activity 7.4 the soil and the water could rise by exactly the same number of degrees, and still a sea breeze would blow in the afternoon. Both start the morning at the same temperature. Show that this cannot happen in the way the chapter explains.
questions.a: A sea breeze needs the land to be warmer than the sea, so that warm air above the land rises and cooler sea air moves in. If both rose by the same number of degrees from the same start, land and sea would be equally warm and there would be no rising warm air above the land to draw the sea air in. In fact soil heats faster, which is why the sea breeze blows.
s: A sea breeze needs warmer land so that air above it rises
Equal rises from the same start leave land and sea equally warm, so nothing draws the air in
Soil really heats faster than water, which is why the breeze exists

questions.q: Write a 24-hour wind log for a coastal town with at least four entries, giving for each the time, the direction of the wind (from the sea or from the land) and the name of the breeze. Add one sentence of reason for the first daytime entry and one for the first night entry.
questions.a: Example: 1 pm, from the sea, sea breeze; 5 pm, from the sea, sea breeze; 11 pm, from the land, land breeze; 4 am, from the land, land breeze. Reason for 1 pm: the land is warmer than the sea, so warm air above the land rises and cooler sea air moves in. Reason for 11 pm: the land has cooled faster, so air above the warmer sea rises and cooler land air moves in. Any consistent log earns full marks.
s: At least four entries with day winds from the sea and night winds from the land
Correct names of the breezes
Valid reasons for one day and one night entry

questions.q:
Match the observation in Column I with the explanation in Column II.
Column I: 1. At 2 pm a kite on a beach is pulled towards the land; 2. At 1 am the same kite is pulled towards the sea; 3. At noon the sand is too hot to stand on but the sea water is pleasant; 4. A hotel in a coastal town has its large windows facing the sea.
Column II: a. Land is warmer than the sea, so cooler sea air moves in; b. Land has cooled faster, so air over the warmer sea rises; c. Land heats faster than water; d. The cool sea breeze is used for relief from the heat.
questions.a: 1 kite towards the land at 2 pm - a (sea breeze); 2 kite towards the sea at 1 am - b (land breeze); 3 hot sand - c; 4 windows facing the sea - d. The other options swap the day and night explanations or the last two.

questions.q: A weather club at a beach in Goa records the temperature of a patch of sand and of the sea water close to it: 6 am, sand 24, sea 27; 9 am, 29 and 28; 1 pm, 41 and 30; 5 pm, 33 and 30; 8 pm, 28 and 29; 11 pm, 25 and 28 (degrees Celsius). At which of the recorded times would the wind near the shore blow from the land towards the sea?
questions.a: A wind blows from the land towards the sea (a land breeze) when the land is cooler than the sea: 24 < 27 at 6 am, 28 < 29 at 8 pm and 25 < 28 at 11 pm. At 9 am, 1 pm and 5 pm the sand is warmer, so the breeze comes from the sea.
o: 6 am, 8 pm and 11 pm
9 am, 1 pm and 5 pm
6 am, 1 pm and 11 pm
1 pm and 5 pm only

questions.q: Two towns record a day high and a night low in degrees Celsius: Town A, 32 and 27; Town B, 41 and 20. One lies on the seashore and the other far inland. Using what Activity 7.4 showed about soil and water, which is more likely to be the seashore town?
questions.a: Town A's day-night difference is 32 - 27 = 5 degrees, Town B's is 41 - 20 = 21 degrees. Water heats and cools more slowly than soil (Activity 7.4), so air close to the sea changes less. This is a reasoned inference from the activity, not a stated rule.
o: Town A, because air near slowly heating and cooling water changes less between day and night
Town B, because land heats and cools faster than water, so the air above it varies much less
Town A, because water heats up faster than soil, so a seashore is always warmer even at night
Town B, because a sea breeze makes the afternoons hotter near the sea

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Sea breeze gives relief from the heat in hot coastal places.
Reason (R): Windows of houses in coastal areas are placed facing the sea.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the windows' direction is a use made of the breeze; it does not explain why the sea breeze gives relief (cooler air moves from the sea to the land).
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

questions.q: Which of these would NOT be expected on a beach at 3 am on a clear night?
questions.a: At night the land cools faster than the sea, so the air above the sea is warmer and rises, and the wind blows from the land towards the sea (a land breeze), which would make the flag point towards the sea. A flag pointing towards the land would indicate a sea breeze.
o: A hotel flag pointing from the sea towards the land
The sand being cooler than the sea water along the same beach
Air above the warmer sea rising, with cooler air moving in
A wind blowing from the land towards the sea across the beach

questions.q: In Activity 7.4 both bowls start at 27 degrees Celsius. After 20 minutes in the Sun the soil reads 47 and the water reads 32. The temperature rise of the soil is ___ times the rise of the water.

Read the statements.
Statement 1: At 2 pm on a sunny day, the air above a beach is warmer than the air above the nearby sea.
Statement 2: At 2 am, cooler air moves from the sea towards the land, because the sea has cooled faster than the land.
Statement 3: When the soil and water of Activity 7.4 are kept indoors for 20 minutes, the soil falls by more degrees than the water.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: the land cools faster than the sea at night, so cooler air moves from the land towards the sea.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A small island lies in the middle of a wide sea. On a hot, sunny afternoon a visitor finds that the wind blows towards the island from every side of the shore. Which statement explains this best?
questions.a: In the daytime land heats faster than water, so the air above the island rises and cooler air from the sea moves in to take its place. Every shore is sea, so the sea breeze comes from every side.
o: The island's land is warmer than the sea, so its warm air rises and cooler sea air moves in
The sea is warmer than the island, so warm sea air rises and pushes the cooler air towards the island
The island cools faster than the sea in the afternoon, so cool island air spreads out over the sea
Land and sea are equally warm in the afternoon, so air moves in from all sides to fill the empty space

questions.q: At a beach town the sea breeze is faint at 10 am, strong at 2 pm, and has died down to nothing around 7 pm before the wind turns round. (a) Why is the sea breeze stronger at 2 pm than at 10 am? (b) Why must the wind drop to nothing before it reverses?
questions.a: (a) By 2 pm the land has heated more than the sea, so the difference in temperature, and the amount of warm air rising over the land, is greater. (b) Around the changeover the land has cooled until it is about as warm as the sea, so there is no warmer side and no rising air to draw the wind; after that the sea is warmer and the land breeze begins.
s: Part (a): the land-sea difference is greater at 2 pm
Part (b): at the changeover land and sea are about equally warm, so no wind, then the sea becomes warmer

questions.q: True or False: Soil heats up faster than water in sunlight, so the air above a beach is always warmer than the air above the sea, day and night. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The statement holds only in the daytime. The land also cools faster than water, so at night the land is cooler than the sea and the air above the sea is warmer. That is why the wind direction reverses between day and night.
s: Verdict: False
Reason or correction: land also cools faster, so at night the air above the sea is warmer

questions.q: Pema sets up Activity 7.4 with a bowl of soil and a bowl of water. (a) Why must the bowls be identical and kept in the same sunlight? (b) Which two numbers does she compare to say which heated faster?
questions.a: (a) So that the only difference between the bowls is what is in them; otherwise a difference in size or sunlight could cause the different temperature changes. (b) The rise in temperature of the soil and the rise of the water in the same 20 minutes.
s: Part (a): identical bowls and sunlight so that only the material differs
Part (b): compares the rises in temperature of soil and water in the same time

questions.q: In the Sun, the temperature of the water in a bowl rises by 6 degrees Celsius in the time the soil in an identical bowl rises by 3 times as many degrees. Both start at 29 degrees. (a) Find the final temperature of each. (b) By how many degrees is the soil then warmer than the water, and what will the air above a patch of land do when the land is this much warmer than the sea?
questions.a: (a) Water 29 + 6 = 35; soil 29 + 18 = 47 degrees. (b) The soil is 47 - 35 = 12 degrees warmer. The air above the warmer land rises and cooler air from the sea moves towards the land.
s: Part (a): 35 and 47 degrees
Part (b): 12 degrees warmer; the air over the land rises and cooler sea air moves in

questions.q: Kamal, a fisherman, sails out of his village harbour at 4 am and returns at 3 pm, using the wind both ways. (a) From which direction (land or sea) does the wind blow at 4 am, and at 3 pm? (b) Explain the 4 am wind.
questions.a: (a) At 4 am the wind blows from the land towards the sea; at 3 pm it blows from the sea towards the land. (b) At night the land cools faster than the sea, so the air above the sea is warmer and rises, and cooler air from the land moves towards the sea.
s: Part (a): land to sea at 4 am; sea to land at 3 pm
Part (b): land has cooled faster, so air over the warmer sea rises and land air moves in

questions.q:
At a school in Chennai, two identical bowls hold soil and water, each with a thermometer. Both start at 31 degrees Celsius and are kept in sunlight for 20 minutes. The soil reaches 49 and the water 36. The bowls are then taken indoors for 20 minutes, when the soil reads 32 and the water 34. A student says: 'My soil was hotter than the water, so the land near the sea must stay warmer than the sea even at midnight.'
(a) Find the rise in temperature of the soil and of the water in sunlight, and the fall of each indoors.
(b) By how many degrees was the soil warmer than the water at the end of the sunlight, and what is the position after 20 minutes indoors?
(c) What do the results show about heating and cooling of land and water?
(d) Is the student's claim correct? Judge it using your answers and name the wind at midnight.
questions.a: (a) Rises: soil 49 - 31 = 18, water 36 - 31 = 5. Falls: soil 49 - 32 = 17, water 36 - 34 = 2. (b) After sunlight the soil was 49 - 36 = 13 degrees warmer; after 20 minutes indoors it is 34 - 32 = 2 degrees cooler than the water. (c) Soil heats faster and cools faster than water. (d) No. The soil became cooler than the water, so at night the land is cooler than the sea, the air above the sea is warmer and rises, and a land breeze blows from land to sea.
s: Part (a): rises 18 and 5, falls 17 and 2
Part (b): 13 warmer, then 2 cooler than the water
Part (c): soil heats and cools faster than water
Part (d): rejects the claim from the readings; land breeze at midnight

questions.q:
A coastal school in Visakhapatnam notes that the sea breeze blows from about 10 am to 4 pm and the land breeze from about 7 pm to 6 am. It can afford one large ventilation window only. A classroom block with 120 students is used from 9 am to 2 pm; a hostel dormitory with 40 students is used from 9 pm to 6 am. A window on the sea side will bring cooler air only while the sea breeze blows, and a window on the land side only while the land breeze blows. The school gives the window to the room with the greater number of student-hours of use during the time its breeze blows.
(a) Name the wind that blows into a sea-facing window and the one that blows into a land-facing window, and say when each blows.
(b) Explain why the wind reverses at night.
(c) For how many hours of use does the classroom overlap the sea breeze, and the dormitory the land breeze?
(d) Work out the student-hours for each room and decide where the window should go.
questions.a: (a) A sea-facing window receives the sea breeze (10 am to 4 pm); a land-facing window receives the land breeze (7 pm to 6 am). (b) At night the land cools faster than the sea, so the air above the sea is warmer and rises, and cooler air from the land moves towards the sea. (c) The classroom is used 9 am to 2 pm, so it overlaps the sea breeze from 10 am to 2 pm = 4 hours; the dormitory is used 9 pm to 6 am = 9 hours, all within the land breeze. (d) Classroom 4 x 120 = 480 student-hours; dormitory 9 x 40 = 360. The classroom has more, so the window goes on the sea side of the classroom.
s: Part (a): sea breeze 10 am to 4 pm; land breeze 7 pm to 6 am
Part (b): land cools faster, air over the warmer sea rises
Part (c): 4 hours and 9 hours
Part (d): 480 against 360 student-hours, so the classroom window on the sea side

questions.q: The day high and night low of two towns with similar sunshine are: seashore Town S, 31 and 27 degrees Celsius; inland Town I, 40 and 21. (i) Find the day-night difference for each. (ii) Using Activity 7.4, explain why the seashore town is likely to have the smaller difference. (iii) Say which wind brings relief to Town S in the daytime and why. (iv) Say what happens to the wind direction at Town S at night. (v) Give a reason why the data alone do not prove that a sea is the cause.
questions.a: (i) S: 31 - 27 = 4 degrees; I: 40 - 21 = 19 degrees. (ii) Soil heats and cools faster than water, so air close to land changes more; the sea changes more slowly, so air near it changes less (an inference from the activity). (iii) The sea breeze: the land is warmer, its air rises and cooler air from the sea moves in. (iv) It reverses to a land breeze, since the land cools faster than the sea. (v) Only two towns are compared; other factors such as cloud or height could also differ, so the data only suggest the cause.
s: Part (i): 4 and 19 degrees
Part (ii): water changes temperature more slowly than land
Part (iii): the sea breeze, cooler air from sea to land by day
Part (iv): reverses to a land breeze at night
Part (v): two towns are too few to prove the cause; other factors could differ

questions.q: A student writes: 'At night the sea cools faster than the land because water loses heat quickly, so the air over the land is warmer and rises. The wind then blows from the sea to the land, and this is called the land breeze.' Evaluate her answer: find each mistake, correct it and give the correct explanation.
questions.a: Mistake 1: it is the land that cools faster than water, not the sea. Mistake 2: so the air above the sea, not the land, is warmer and rises. Mistake 3: the cooler air moves from the land towards the sea, not from the sea to the land. A wind from the sea to the land is a sea breeze, which blows in the day. Correct explanation: at night the land cools faster, the air above the warmer sea rises, and cooler air from the land moves towards the sea: a land breeze.
s: Corrects: the land cools faster than the sea
Corrects: the air above the sea is the warmer air that rises
Corrects: the wind blows from the land to the sea
Points out that a sea-to-land wind is the daytime sea breeze
Gives the complete correct explanation of the land breeze

questions.q: On a cold morning in Shimla, Meena stands in bright sunshine and her face feels warm, although the air around her is measured at only 4 degrees Celsius. Which statement explains the warmth she feels?
questions.a: Heat from the Sun reaches us by radiation, which needs no medium and does not depend on the air being warm. The measured air temperature of 4 degrees rules out heated air as the source.
o: The Sun's heat reaches her directly by radiation, even though the air around her is cold
The air around her has been heated to a high temperature by convection and carries the heat to her face
The Sun's heat reaches her by conduction through the cold air between the Sun and her face
The Sun's heat warms the ground first and the ground passes the heat to her face by conduction

questions.q:
Match the observation in Column I with the explanation in Column II.
Column I: 1. A hand held beside, not touching, a glowing coal stove feels warm; 2. The end of an iron poker left in the coals becomes too hot to hold; 3. Smoke from the coals drifts up to the ceiling; 4. A person in a white kurta feels cooler in the Sun than one in a black kurta.
Column II: a. Most of the heat falling on the cloth is reflected; b. Heat comes directly from the glowing object without any medium; c. Heat is passed from particle to particle of a solid; d. Warmer gases and particles move upward and carry the heat.
questions.a: 1 hand beside the stove - b (radiation); 2 iron poker - c (conduction); 3 smoke - d (convection); 4 white kurta - a (light surfaces reflect most of the heat). The other options swap the processes.

questions.q: Ravi heats milk in a steel pan on a gas flame. (1) The steel handle of the pan slowly becomes warm. (2) The milk gets warm throughout. (3) Standing to the side, Ravi feels warmth on his face. Which option gives the process for (1), (2) and (3) in order?
questions.a: The handle is a solid whose particles pass the heat on (conduction). The milk is a liquid in which heated milk rises and cooler milk comes down (convection). The warmth felt at the side without contact comes directly from the hot pan and flame (radiation).
o: Conduction, convection, radiation
Convection, conduction, radiation
Conduction, radiation, convection
Radiation, convection, conduction

questions.q: Neeta sits near a bonfire and feels its warmth on her face. Which observation would best show that the warmth reaches her by radiation and not by convection?
questions.a: If the warmth is still felt when the hot air is blown away from her, the heat cannot be coming with moving air, so it is radiation. The other observations are consistent with both processes or with neither.
o: She still feels the warmth when wind blows the hot air away from her
Smoke and flames can be seen rising steadily above the fire into the sky
Her face feels warmer than her back, which faces away from the fire
The grass and the ground nearest to the fire are burnt black

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A person sitting beside a fire can feel its warmth even when no hot air moves towards the person, because radiation needs no medium.
Statement 2: Of the three processes of heat transfer, only radiation can carry heat across a region that contains no matter.
Statement 3: In winter a dark jacket worn in sunlight takes in more of the Sun's heat than a light jacket does, which is why it feels more comfortable.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three are correct. Radiation needs no medium, while conduction and convection need particles; and dark surfaces absorb more heat while light ones reflect most of it.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Palden holds one hand 15 cm above a lit candle and the other hand 15 cm to its side. Both hands feel warm, and the hand above feels warmer. Which explanation is best?
questions.a: Radiation reaches both hands directly from the flame without a medium. The hand above is also in the stream of hot air that rises from the flame (convection), so it gets heat by two routes.
o: Both hands receive heat by radiation; the hand above also gets heat from rising hot air
Only conduction through the air warms the hand above, because the air at the side is not touching the flame
The hand at the side is warmed by convection and the hand above is warmed by radiation
Radiation travels only upwards from a flame, so the hand at the side is warmed by the rising air

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Dark-coloured clothes are more comfortable in winter.
Reason (R): Woollen fabric traps air in its pores.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. Woollen fabric trapping air is a fact about wool; it does not explain why dark surfaces, which absorb more heat, are comfortable in winter.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

questions.q: Two identical steel bottles of water, one painted white and one painted black, are left in the same sunlight. The water in the white bottle warms by 5 degrees Celsius and the water in the black bottle by 15. The black bottle warmed ___ times as much as the white one.

A school in Jaisalmer gives its students caps for the outdoor assembly in May, when the sunshine is strong, and for the January assembly on bright but cold mornings. (a) Should the cap colour be light or dark in each month? (b) Give the reason for each choice.
questions.a: (a) Light in May, dark in January. (b) Light-coloured surfaces reflect most of the heat falling on them, so they are more comfortable in summer; dark surfaces absorb more heat, so they are more comfortable in winter.
s: Part (a): light in May, dark in January
Part (b): light reflects most heat, dark absorbs more

questions.q: Rina says the Sun's heat reaches the Earth by convection, carried by hot gases flowing from the Sun. Sana says it reaches us by radiation. (a) Whose view agrees with the book? (b) Using what each process needs, explain why the other view cannot be right.
questions.a: (a) Sana's. (b) Convection is heat carried by the actual movement of particles, so it needs a medium; radiation needs no medium. The Sun's heat crosses the large gap to the Earth without any medium having to carry it, so it must be radiation.
s: Part (a): Sana, radiation
Part (b): convection needs a medium of moving particles; radiation needs none

questions.q: At a dhaba a customer stands 1 m from a glowing tandoor and feels strong warmth on her face. A thermometer held in the air at her face reads 31 degrees Celsius, in a room at 30. (a) Can hot air be the main source of the warmth she feels? Give a reason from the reading. (b) Name the process that brings the heat to her.
questions.a: (a) No: the air at her face is only 1 degree above the room's temperature, so it carries very little heat. (b) Radiation: heat travels directly from the hot tandoor with no medium.
s: Part (a): no, the air is barely warmer than the room
Part (b): radiation

questions.q: True or False: A block of ice kept in a warm room gives out heat by radiation too, even though it is cold. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. All objects radiate heat and exchange heat with their surroundings by radiation, not only hot ones. The ice melts because it takes in more heat from its warmer surroundings than it gives out.
s: Verdict: True
Reason or correction: every object radiates heat; the ice gains more than it gives

questions.q: With no wind, thermometers are placed 0.5 m, 1 m and 2 m to the side of a burning angithi (coal stove) in a room at 30 degrees Celsius. They read 41, 35 and 31. (a) Find the rise above room temperature at each position. (b) Name the process by which the heat reaches these thermometers and say what the readings show about distance from the stove.
questions.a: (a) 11, 5 and 1 degrees. (b) Radiation: heat travels directly from the stove, without hot air moving sideways. The farther the thermometer is from the stove, the smaller the rise in temperature.
s: Part (a): 11, 5 and 1 degrees
Part (b): radiation, with the rise getting smaller farther from the stove

questions.q: You have a candle, a metal strip with pins stuck by wax, a beaker of water with a grain of potassium permanganate, and a thermometer. Plan three short demonstrations, one each for conduction, convection and radiation. For each, say what you will do and what you will see, and say how an observer can tell the three processes apart.
questions.a: Conduction: heat one end of the strip and see the pins fall one after another, the nearest first; the particles stay in place. Convection: heat the beaker below its centre and see the coloured streak rise in the middle and come down at the sides, the water itself moving. Radiation: hold a thermometer to the side of the flame, with no hot air moving to it, and see its reading rise without any contact. To tell them apart: conduction needs touching particles that stay in place, convection needs moving particles of a liquid or gas, radiation needs no medium. Supervision by a teacher or adult is needed for the flame.
s: Conduction demonstration with its observation
Convection demonstration with its observation
Radiation demonstration with its observation
Tells them apart by what moves and whether a medium is needed
Mentions supervision or care with the flame

questions.q: Two students argue about how the Sun's heat reaches the Earth. Tara says it comes by conduction, through the air, like heat along a spoon. Uday says it comes by convection, with hot gases flowing from the Sun. Evaluate both views using what each process needs, and state the process the book gives, with one more everyday example of that process.
questions.a: Conduction passes heat from particle to particle in a medium, so it needs matter all the way, and Tara's view fails because heat cannot be passed on without particles between the Sun and the Earth. Convection needs particles that actually move and carry the heat, so it also needs a medium, and Uday's view fails for the same reason. The book says the Sun's heat reaches the Earth by radiation, which needs no medium. Another example of radiation: the warmth felt around a fire, or a hot utensil cooling by radiating heat to its surroundings.
s: Conduction needs particles to pass the heat on, a medium
Tara's view fails because a medium is needed all the way
Convection needs moving particles, a medium, so Uday's view fails too
Radiation is the process the book gives; it needs no medium
A correct everyday example of radiation

questions.q: A student says a white and a black cotton T-shirt of the same size, spread in the same sunlight for 30 minutes, must end up at the same temperature. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: Light-coloured surfaces reflect most of the heat that falls on them, while dark surfaces absorb more of it. The two shirts receive the same sunlight, but the black one absorbs more and the white one reflects more, so the black shirt must become hotter. The same cloth and sunlight do not give the same temperature.
s: Light surfaces reflect most of the heat falling on them
Dark surfaces absorb more of the heat
So the black shirt must end up hotter, despite the same sunlight

questions.q: Give one situation, not in the chapter, where you feel heat by radiation. Say how you can tell that it is not conduction or convection.
questions.a: Example: standing beside a hot tandoor or a lit lamp and feeling the warmth on the skin without touching it. Not conduction because nothing touches the body; not convection because the warmth is felt from the side by direct transfer, not through moving hot air.
s: A valid situation of radiation
Reason that it is not conduction
Reason that it is not convection

questions.q: Imran says: 'At a bonfire I feel its warmth on my face although the hot air from the fire is rising upward. If all the air between the fire and me were removed, I would still feel the warmth.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. Since the hot air rises upward and does not blow to him, the warmth cannot be carried to him by convection. The warmth reaches him by radiation, which needs no medium, so removing the air would make no difference. Only conduction and convection need a medium.
s: Verdict: agrees
The rising hot air does not carry the warmth to him, so it is radiation
Radiation needs no medium, unlike conduction and convection

questions.q:
A family in Kullu keeps a bukhari in its winter room, which is at 10 degrees Celsius before the stove is lit. After an hour, thermometers read 24 degrees at 1 m to the side of the stove, 18 degrees at 2 m to the side, and 32 degrees in the air just below the ceiling above the stove. The hot air rises straight up and does not blow sideways. Grandmother must sit in a place that is at least 20 degrees and not directly above the stove.
(a) By how many degrees did the air at each position rise above the starting 10 degrees?
(b) Name the process by which the places at the side get their warmth, and give a reason from the passage.
(c) Name the process that makes the air below the ceiling the warmest, and explain it.
(d) Where should Grandmother sit? Check each place against her two conditions.
questions.a: (a) 1 m side: 24 - 10 = 14 degrees; 2 m side: 18 - 10 = 8; ceiling: 32 - 10 = 22. (b) Radiation: the hot air does not blow sideways, so the heat reaches the side directly from the stove without a medium. (c) Convection: air heated by the stove expands, becomes lighter and rises, carrying heat to the ceiling. (d) At 1 m to the side: 24 is above 20 and it is not above the stove.
