The 2 m place (18) is too cool, and the warmest place, below the ceiling, is directly above the stove and cannot be used for sitting.
s: Part (a): 14, 8 and 22 degrees
Part (b): radiation, since the hot air does not blow sideways
Part (c): convection, hot air expands, becomes lighter and rises
Part (d): 1 m to the side; 2 m is too cool and the ceiling place is above the stove

questions.q:
The sports committee of a Jaipur school tests T-shirts on a May afternoon. Cotton T-shirts start in the shade of the tent at 38 degrees Celsius and are then spread in the Sun for 30 minutes. A white one reads 42, a black one reads 52 and a white one with a narrow black band reads 43. Shivaji House wants its black identity, so it considers only black shirts or white shirts with the black band. A black T-shirt costs Rs 300; a white one costs Rs 240, and printing the band costs Rs 90 more. The house needs 40 shirts, has Rs 13,500, and will accept only a shirt that stays at 45 degrees or below.
(a) Find the rise in temperature for the white and for the black T-shirt, and how much hotter the black one got.
(b) Explain the difference between them using reflection and absorption of heat.
(c) Which of the two options meets the 45-degree rule?
(d) Find the cost of 40 shirts of each option and decide which the committee should buy.
questions.a: (a) White 42 - 38 = 4, black 52 - 38 = 14 degrees; the black shirt got 52 - 42 = 10 degrees hotter. (b) The white shirt reflects most of the heat falling on it, while the black one absorbs more. (c) The white shirt with the band (43) meets the rule; the black shirt (52) does not. (d) 40 black shirts cost 40 x 300 = Rs 12,000, but fail the rule. 40 white shirts with a band cost 40 x (240 + 90) = Rs 13,200, within Rs 13,500 and Rs 1,200 more than black. Buy the white shirts with the black band: they keep the team's identity and meet the comfort rule.
s: Part (a): 4 and 14 degrees; 10 degrees hotter
Part (b): light reflects most heat, dark absorbs more
Part (c): the white shirt with the band meets the rule; black does not
Part (d): Rs 12,000 and Rs 13,200; buy white with the band as it meets the rule within budget

questions.q: The flat roof of a school in Pune has an area of 80 square metres and 0.75 m of rain falls on it in a monsoon. 1 cubic metre of water is 1,000 litres. (a) Find the volume of rainwater falling on the roof, in litres. (b) If this water is led into a recharge pit instead of the drain, name the process by which it enters the ground and the underground store in which it collects.
questions.a: (a) 80 x 0.75 = 60 cubic metres = 60,000 litres. (b) Infiltration; the water is stored as groundwater in an aquifer.
s: Part (a): 60 cubic metres, i.e. 60,000 litres
Part (b): infiltration, stored in an aquifer

questions.q: True or False: Water drawn from a well in summer may have fallen as rain during an earlier monsoon, so harvesting rainwater today can help the wells of the coming years. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Rainwater that seeps into the ground is stored as groundwater in aquifers, from which wells draw water. Recharge pits and rainwater harvesting add to this store, so rain that falls and seeps in now can supply wells later.
s: Verdict: True
Reason or correction: seepage stores rainwater in aquifers, which wells use later; harvesting adds to the store

questions.q: To make an ice stupa the villagers send stream water down underground pipes and spray it into the cold air. (a) Why is the water sprayed rather than poured on the ground? (b) Why is the stupa built in winter?
questions.a: (a) Sprayed water falls through the extremely cold air and freezes as it falls, so the ice builds up layer by layer into a cone. (b) In winter the temperature is low enough to freeze it, and the water stored as ice melts slowly in spring when the streams dry up.
s: Part (a): sprayed water freezes as it falls through the cold air, building layers
Part (b): built in winter's low temperatures to supply water when streams dry up in spring

questions.q: The water in a village well stands 9 m deep in June and 14 m deep in October, after the monsoon. (a) By how much did the level rise? (b) Explain the rise using infiltration and the aquifer.
questions.a: (a) 14 - 9 = 5 m. (b) Monsoon rain seeped into the ground by infiltration and was stored in the aquifer from which the well draws water, so the level rose.
s: Part (a): 5 m
Part (b): rain infiltrated and recharged the aquifer

questions.q: A rock has many tiny holes, but none of them is joined to another. (a) Can it store water in its pores? (b) Why would a well drilled into it give very little water?
questions.a: (a) Yes, the pores can hold water. (b) Water moves readily only where the spaces are wide, open and interconnected; with unconnected holes it cannot flow to the well, so it gives little water.
s: Part (a): the pores can hold some water
Part (b): water moves readily only through interconnected spaces

questions.q: Describe a situation near a town, not given in the chapter, in which human activity reduces infiltration of rainwater, and suggest one measure that improves it. Use the chapter's idea of what lets water seep in.
questions.a: Example: a new housing colony covers its lanes and courtyards with concrete, so rain runs into drains and cannot seep in. A measure: leave open ground or build recharge pits so rainwater can infiltrate and refill the aquifer. Water infiltrates readily where the spaces between particles are wide, open and interconnected, and concrete closes them. Any valid situation and measure with the reason earns full marks.
s: A valid situation that reduces infiltration
A valid measure such as recharge pits or open ground
Reason from wide, open, interconnected spaces letting water seep in

questions.q: Show why continuous evaporation of water from oceans, rivers and lakes does not use up the Earth's water.
questions.a: The water vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds. Precipitation brings it back down as rain, snow and hail, and it flows through soil, rocks and plants to return to water bodies. The water cycle conserves the total amount of water on the Earth.
s: Vapour condenses into clouds
Precipitation returns the water to the Earth
Water returns to water bodies; the cycle conserves the total water

questions.q: Zubin says: 'Rainwater that seeps into the ground is lost to the water cycle; only the water that flows into rivers goes back to the oceans.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The water cycle includes the downward movement of water through soil, rocks and plants, finally returning to water bodies. The seeped water is stored as groundwater in aquifers, can be drawn out through wells, and the cycle recharges these sources again. So seepage is a part of the water cycle, not a loss.
s: Verdict: disagrees
The cycle includes water passing through soil, rocks and plants and returning to water bodies
Seeped water is stored as groundwater which can be used, and the cycle recharges it

questions.q: On a dry, sunny day the air over a thick forest holds more water vapour than the air over bare ground nearby. Besides evaporation from the soil and water, which process adds the extra vapour?
questions.a: Water also evaporates from trees and plants through transpiration. Condensation, infiltration and precipitation do not put vapour into the air.
o: Transpiration, the loss of water vapour from trees and plants
Condensation, which turns the water in the leaves into vapour
Infiltration, which carries groundwater up into the air
Precipitation, which lifts water from the leaves into the clouds

questions.q: In a repeat of Activity 7.5, 200 mL of water is poured into each bottle. After 10 minutes the beakers hold 20 mL (clay), 90 mL (sand) and 160 mL (gravel). A fourth bottle, filled with gravel mixed with clay, gives 60 mL. Which statement best fits this result?
questions.a: The mixture lets through far less than pure gravel (60 against 160 mL) but more than pure clay (20 mL). Water seeps more readily where the spaces are wide, open and interconnected, and the clay narrows them.
o: The clay fills some of the wide spaces between the gravel, so less water passes through
Mixed material always lets exactly the average of its two parts through, so 60 mL is expected
Clay opens the spaces between gravel particles, so the mixture should let more water through
The mixture holds back no water, since the water flows around the clay lumps

questions.q: In a repeat of Activity 7.5, 200 mL of water is poured into each bottle. After 10 minutes the gravel bottle's beaker holds 140 mL and the clay bottle's beaker holds 10 mL. The gravel bottle has let through ___ times as much water as the clay bottle.

Assertion (A): Digging a recharge pit on a paved school ground can raise the water level in the school's well.
Reason (R): Rainwater led into the pit seeps through soil and rocks and is stored as groundwater in the aquifer.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and the Reason explains the Assertion: the pit lets rain infiltrate and replenish the aquifer from which the well draws water, instead of running off over the concrete.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Water that seeps into the ground is lost from the water cycle for ever, so the cycle cannot refill groundwater.
Statement 2: A compound with trees and bare soil lets more rainwater infiltrate than the same compound covered with concrete, so its wells are more likely to be refilled.
Statement 3: Groundwater will be found at the same depth below the ground in every town.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only Statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is false: the water cycle recharges groundwater sources. Statement 3 is false: the water may be a few metres to hundreds of metres below the ground, depending on the location.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: Three colonies in one town get the same rainfall and have the same number of residents using the same amount of water from their wells. Over ten years the well level fell by 12 m in Colony P, where 80 per cent of the ground is now paved; by 5 m in Colony Q, 40 per cent paved; and by 1 m in Colony R, 10 per cent paved. Which conclusion do these data support best?
questions.a: With rainfall and use equal, the fall rises with the paved share (1, 5, 12 m for 10, 40, 80 per cent). The book says increased concrete surfaces limit water infiltration, so less rain refills the aquifer.
o: The more ground is paved, the more the well level fell, fitting concrete limiting infiltration
Paving makes rainwater run faster into the wells, so wells in paved colonies should fall less
The fall depends on the rainfall each colony got, since colonies with more concrete get less rain
The wells fell by different amounts only because the aquifers hold different kinds of water

questions.q: A school ground has a thick layer of clay just below the surface, and beneath it a layer of gravel. Rainwater stands on the surface for hours. Why will digging a recharge pit through the clay into the gravel help?
questions.a: Water seeps slowest through clay and fastest through gravel because gravel's spaces are wider. The pit takes the water past the clay and into the gravel, from which it can replenish groundwater.
o: Clay lets water seep slowly, so the pit takes rainwater down to the gravel, where it seeps easily
Clay lets water seep faster than gravel, so the pit will make use of the clay at its sides and bottom
Gravel holds back water, so the pit fills with water and keeps it from reaching the aquifer below
The pit adds new water to the ground, as the cycle makes more water on the Earth over the years

questions.q: In Ladakh, villagers build ice stupas in winter and not in spring. Which is the best reason?
questions.a: In winter, water from the mountain streams is sprayed into the very cold air and freezes layer by layer. In spring the streams often dry up, so there would be nothing to freeze; the stupa melts slowly in spring and supplies water.
o: In winter the streams flow and the cold air freezes the spray, while in spring they dry up
In spring the Sun's heat is too weak to melt snow, so stupas would melt immediately
In winter the stupa creates new water from the cold air, which the dry streams cannot supply
In spring the water cycle stops, so no water can be stored in any form at all

questions.q: A student writes: 'The Sun heats the sea and the vapour rises and forms clouds. The clouds drop rain on the land. All the rain flows into rivers and goes back to the sea. Groundwater is formed only when rivers dry up, and it can never run out.' Evaluate this account: say what is correct, find the mistakes and correct them.
questions.a: Correct: the Sun's heat evaporates sea water, the vapour rises and condenses into clouds, and the clouds bring rain. Mistake 1: not all the rain flows into rivers; some seeps into the ground by infiltration. Mistake 2: groundwater is formed by this seepage, with water stored in the pore spaces of sediments and rocks in aquifers, not when rivers dry up. Mistake 3: groundwater is not unlimited; excessive extraction and decreased infiltration deplete it, and recharge pits and harvesting help to replenish it.
s: Identifies the correct part: evaporation, condensation and rain
Corrects: some rain seeps in by infiltration
Corrects: groundwater forms from the seepage and is stored in aquifers
Corrects: groundwater is not unlimited and can be depleted
Mentions recharge pits or harvesting to replenish

questions.q: One village has mostly sandy soil and another mostly clay soil. The same rain falls on both. Predict which village will recharge its groundwater faster, explain why, say what may happen to the rest of the rainwater in the other village, and suggest one measure to recharge groundwater there.
questions.a: The sandy village recharges faster: water seeps more readily through sand than through clay because the spaces between sand particles are wider. In the clay village water seeps slowest, so rainwater can flow into ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans instead of seeping. The clay village can use rainwater harvesting or recharge pits to replenish groundwater.
s: Predicts the sandy village recharges faster
Reason: wider spaces between sand particles than clay
Clay seeps slowest, so water seeps in less
Rest of the rain flows to ponds, lakes and rivers
A recharge measure such as pits or rainwater harvesting

questions.q:
A village in Satara depends on one open well. The water stood 8 metres below the ground in 2015 and 21 metres below the ground in 2025, though the yearly rainfall was about the same. The village square and lanes have been covered with concrete over these years. The panchayat has Rs 1,50,000. Recharge pits near the square cost Rs 1,20,000 and Rs 4,000 a year to maintain; they would start refilling the aquifer only after the next monsoon, 8 months away. A pipeline from a river 12 km away costs Rs 1,40,000 and Rs 18,000 a year to run. At the present use the well will last 10 more months. The panchayat decides on the 10-year total cost, provided the water does not run out before help arrives.
(a) By how many metres has the water level fallen?
(b) Explain why paving the square could lower the well level though the rainfall stayed the same.
(c) Explain how the recharge pits help the aquifer.
(d) Work out the 10-year cost of each option and decide which the panchayat should choose.
questions.a: (a) 21 - 8 = 13 metres. (b) Concrete limits infiltration, so less rainwater seeps down to refill the aquifer. (c) Rainwater led into the pits infiltrates into the ground and replenishes the aquifer. (d) Pits: 1,20,000 + 10 x 4,000 = Rs 1,60,000. Pipeline: 1,40,000 + 10 x 18,000 = Rs 3,20,000. The pits cost Rs 1,60,000 less, and the well lasts 10 months while the pits start helping in 8 months, so the water will not run out. Choose the recharge pits.
s: Part (a): 13 metres
Part (b): concrete limits infiltration
Part (c): rainwater infiltrates and replenishes the aquifer
Part (d): Rs 1,60,000 against Rs 3,20,000, and 8 months is less than 10 months, so pits

In a Ladakh village the streams dry up in spring because the heat of the Sun's radiation is not enough to melt the snow on the mountains. In winter the villagers channel stream water down underground pipes and spray it into the cold air, where it freezes into an ice stupa. The stupa holds 1,50,000 litres of water as ice. The fields need 2,500 litres a day in spring and the dry spell lasts 90 days. The crops fail if they get less than 2,000 litres a day. A second stupa, holding 75,000 litres, costs Rs 40,000; the village has Rs 45,000.
(a) For how many days will the first stupa's water last at 2,500 litres a day?
(b) When does the stupa melt, and why is it useful then?
(c) How many more litres are needed to cover all 90 days, and does the second stupa cover them?
(d) If instead the villagers cut the daily use so that the first stupa lasts 90 days, find the daily amount to the nearest 10 litres and decide which option to choose.
questions.a: (a) 1,50,000 / 2,500 = 60 days. (b) The stupa melts slowly during spring, when the streams have dried up, and provides water for farming. (c) 90 x 2,500 = 2,25,000 litres are needed, so 2,25,000 - 1,50,000 = 75,000 litres more; the second stupa holds exactly 75,000 litres, so it covers them. (d) 1,50,000 / 90 = about 1,670 litres a day, which is less than the 2,000 litres below which crops fail. So cutting use is not acceptable; build the second stupa for Rs 40,000, within the Rs 45,000 the village has.
s: Part (a): 60 days
Part (b): melts slowly in spring, when streams are dry
Part (c): 75,000 litres, which the second stupa provides
Part (d): about 1,670 litres a day is below 2,000, so build the second stupa for Rs 40,000
